corrections.metricOrTopic: Pelland 2025 study size and counting method
corrections.claim: Bayesian meta-regression of 67 studies and 2,058 participants; 'fractional' counting (indirect set = 0.5) fitted best
corrections.correction: Confirmed. Detail: the hypertrophy volume model itself used 35 studies, 220 effects and 1,032 participants; the strength model used 66 studies and 2,020 participants. Europe PMC lists the issue year as Sports Med 2026 (published online in 2025).
corrections.source: Pelland et al., Sports Med (PMID 41343037), abstract via Europe PMC + full-text PDF §3.6.1–3.6.2

corrections.claim: MED 4; 5–10 ~6 sets per extra detectable gain; 11–18 ~8.5; 19–29 ~10.75; 30–42 ~12.5; 43+ no data
corrections.correction: Matches Table 3 exactly. The smallest detectable effect size for hypertrophy is 2.05%. The best-fit model is a square root, with diminishing returns and no clear plateau. Few studies tested ~25+ sets.
corrections.source: Pelland 2025 full text, Table 3 and Discussion

corrections.claim: MED 1 set; higher efficiency at 2; intermediate at 3–4; no consistent gain above detection from 5; detection threshold 3.96%; reciprocal model with functional plateau
corrections.correction: Matches Table 4. The 'higher efficiency' tier is 2 sets (~0.75 extra sets per detectable gain), and 'intermediate' is 3–4 sets (~2.25).

corrections.claim: Strength: fractional frequency 1 → ES 12.72%, 2 → 17.32%; hypertrophy posterior probability <100%
corrections.correction: Confirmed: 12.72% (95% CrI 10.57–15.05) to 17.32% (CrI from 14.34). The reciprocal model fitted best for both outcomes.

corrections.claim: Point of undetectable superiority at ~11 fractional sets per session for hypertrophy and ~2 direct sets for strength
corrections.correction: Confirmed in the SportRxiv abstract, 2025. The authors say to interpret it cautiously because data at very high per-session volumes are sparse. It is a preprint and not peer reviewed.

corrections.claim: Each extra weekly set ≈ +0.37% muscle gain (ES +0.023)
corrections.correction: Confirmed (15 studies, 34 treatment groups).
corrections.source: J Sports Sci 2017, PMID 27433992 (Europe PMC abstract)

corrections.claim: Trained men: no difference 12–20 vs >20 sets for quads and biceps; triceps favoured >20; 12–20 recommended
corrections.correction: Confirmed. Small review: 7 studies, 6 of them meta-analysed. Quads p=0.19, biceps p=0.59, triceps p=0.01.

corrections.claim: 137 systematic reviews; hypertrophy enhanced by ≥10 sets/wk; strength by ≥80% 1RM, full ROM, 2–3 sets, early in the session, ≥2 sessions/wk; failure, equipment and set structure not consistently influential
corrections.correction: Confirmed (>30,000 participants). Currier BS is first author. The abstract also names eccentric overload as enhancing hypertrophy.
corrections.source: Med Sci Sports Exerc 2026, PMID 41843416 (Europe PMC)

corrections.claim: 25 studies; no meaningful difference when volume is equated
corrections.correction: Confirmed.

corrections.claim: ES 0.74/0.82/0.93/1.08 for 1/2/3/4+ sessions; no effect when volume equated (p=0.421); 22 studies
corrections.correction: Confirmed.

corrections.claim: 21 studies, all sets to failure; greater 1RM gains with high loads (>60% 1RM); similar hypertrophy
corrections.correction: Confirmed. Low load was defined as ≤60% 1RM. No difference was found for isometric strength.

corrections.claim: 8–12RM novices; periodised 1–12RM with emphasis on 1–6RM and 3–5 min rest for strength; 6–12RM with 1–2 min rest for hypertrophy
corrections.correction: Confirmed against the abstract.

corrections.claim: Per ACSM 2009, raise load 2–10% after 1–2 reps over target: ~2–5% for upper-body or isolation lifts, ~5–10% for lower-body compounds (app rule fires after one qualifying session)
corrections.correction: ACSM gives no 2–5%/5–10% sub-bands and does not say upper vs lower body. The full text reads: 2–10% ('lower percent for small muscle mass exercises, higher percent increase for large muscle mass exercises'), applied when the lifter can do 1–2 reps over target 'on two consecutive training sessions' (Evidence category B). The app's READY-TO-ADD-LOAD rule should require two consecutive qualifying sessions, or be labelled a stricter heuristic. The upper/lower % split is an NSCA-style practitioner convention.
corrections.source: ACSM 2009 full text p.~691 (tourniquets.org mirror PDF of MSSE 41:687-708)

corrections.claim: Strength slopes compatible with zero; hypertrophy slopes negative with CIs excluding zero; exploratory
corrections.correction: Confirmed.

corrections.claim: 15 studies; set failure vs non-failure ES 0.19 (0.00–0.37); momentary failure vs non-failure ES 0.12 (−0.13 to 0.37)
corrections.correction: Confirmed.

corrections.claim: Strength ES −0.09; hypertrophy ES 0.22 n.s.; trained-hypertrophy ES 0.15; non-failure favoured for strength when volume not equated (ES −0.32)
corrections.correction: Confirmed (15 studies, young adults only).

corrections.claim: Reps to failure underpredicted by 0.95 on average; more accurate closer to failure and at ≤12 reps
corrections.correction: Confirmed: 0.95 reps (95% CI 0.17–1.73) across 12 studies and 414 participants, with very high heterogeneity (I²≈98%).

corrections.claim: 8-week RCT in trained lifters; similar hypertrophy, strength and endurance
corrections.correction: Confirmed (n=43, lower body, 2×/week). Rectus femoris growth slightly favoured rep progression and 1RM slightly favoured load progression, both of questionable practical size.

corrections.claim: Varied vs constant exercises: thickness +7.5–19.3% vs +7.8–17.7%; similar 1RM
corrections.correction: Numbers confirmed. Context the app should not overgeneralise: 70 young women, 10 weeks, lower-body only, 2 sets of 10–15RM.

corrections.claim: 15 studies, 8,459 athletes; RR 0.49; RCT-only 0.52
corrections.correction: Confirmed: RR 0.49 (0.32–0.74); 8 RCTs RR 0.52 (0.32–0.85); after removing high risk of bias 0.55.

corrections.claim: 78 studies; older age and prior hamstring injury are the strongest risk factors
corrections.correction: Confirmed: 78 studies, 8,319 injuries, 71,324 athletes. Older age SMD 1.6; prior injury RR 2.7.

corrections.claim: Recreational lifters had greater agonist/antagonist ratios and reduced mobility; training biased to pecs/delts
corrections.correction: Confirmed (90 men: 60 lifters, 30 controls; cross-sectional).

corrections.claim: n=39 trained; 1-week cessation mid 9-week programme: no difference in hypertrophy, power or endurance but smaller lower-body strength gains
corrections.correction: Confirmed (29 men, 10 women; only the lower body was supervised).

corrections.claim: Deloading every 4–6 weeks for ~7 days; 100% agreement on lowering sets; regular 4–8-week deloads precautionary
corrections.correction: All three are verbatim in the full text (the 4–6 week figure is background citing their survey, ref 22).
corrections.source: Sports Med Open 2023, PMC10511399 full text

corrections.claim: Reduced-volume deload: cut sets or reps by ~40–50% and keep the load
corrections.correction: None of the cited sources (Bell 2023, Coleman 2024, Meeusen 2013) gives a 40–50% figure. Bell reports only that coaches reduce sets and/or reps, and that intensity may or may not be kept. Label it a practitioner heuristic.

corrections.claim: No single marker meets all criteria
corrections.correction: Confirmed.

corrections.claim: 16 cohorts; 10–17% lower risk; J-shape with maximum ~10–20% reduction at ~30–60 min/wk; diabetes L-shaped to 60 min; higher volumes unclear
corrections.correction: Confirmed.

corrections.claim: 11 studies, 370,256 participants; RT HR 0.79 (0.69–0.91); RT+aerobic 0.60 (0.49–0.72); CV mortality 0.83 (0.67–1.03)
corrections.correction: Confirmed.

corrections.claim: 150–300 min moderate or 75–150 min vigorous per week plus muscle strengthening
corrections.correction: Confirmed.

corrections.metricOrTopic: ACSM 2011 (Garber) dose and HR intensity bands
corrections.claim: ≥150 min moderate / ≥75 min vigorous; ≥500–1,000 MET-min/wk; moderate 64–76% HRmax, vigorous 77–95%
corrections.correction: Confirmed (abstract; intensity table in the position stand).

corrections.claim: HRmax = 208 − 0.7×age; 351 studies, 18,712 subjects; lab cross-validation n=514; independent of sex and activity
corrections.correction: Confirmed. The lab equation was 209 − 0.7×age, virtually identical.

Values match Table 2. Table 3 repeats the maxima with slightly different SDs (e.g. 30–39 = 49.1±7.7). 3,816 is the title n; the tables analyse 1,929 men + 1,881 women (3,810). Treadmill running with direct gas analysis.

corrections.claim: Rounded means 54/49/47/42/39/34; inactive vs active men 50–59 = 38 vs 47
corrections.correction: Confirmed on the page. It also gives men 20–29 inactive 47 vs active 60.
Confirmed (7,783 treadmill tests, ~10% decline per decade).

corrections.claim: US FRIEND 50th percentile: men 20–29 = 48.0, declining ~4 mL/kg/min per decade in the 2022 update
corrections.correction: 48.0 is the 2015 value. The 2022 update's treadmill standards are 1.5–4.6 mL/kg/min LOWER than 2015, so the 2022 men 20–29 median is below 48.0. The 4.0 mL/kg/min (13.5%) per-decade decline is correct, but for treadmill only; cycle is 4.3 (16.4%). The app must use one version and one test mode (treadmill vs cycle) consistently and not mix the 2015 table with 2022 slopes.

corrections.claim: +1 MET = 13% lower all-cause and 15% lower CHD/CVD risk
corrections.correction: RR 0.87 (0.84–0.90) all-cause and 0.85 (0.82–0.88) CHD/CVD; 33 studies.

corrections.claim: 122,007 treadmill tests; elite vs low adjusted HR 0.20 (0.16–0.24); no upper limit
corrections.correction: Confirmed. Caveats: patients referred for clinical exercise testing; CRF estimated from treadmill workload (METs), not measured VO2.

corrections.claim: n=40; mean difference −6.25; LoA −18.23 to 5.73; MAE 6.79; MAPE 13.2%; correct FRIEND band in only 14%
corrections.correction: Confirmed. The 14% is 5 participants; a further 34% were within one adjacent band.
corrections.source: Mayo Clin Proc Digit Health 2026, PMID 42094313

corrections.claim: n=30; underestimation 6.07; MAE 6.92; MAPE 13.31%
corrections.correction: Figures confirmed (the abstract's LoA are −6.11 to 18.26 in lab-minus-watch sign). 30 were recruited and 28 analysed.

corrections.metricOrTopic: Applying the Apple Watch bias to a low-fitness user
corrections.claim: The owner's low VO2max may be partly measurement error; show 'Apple tended to read ~6 low'
corrections.correction: The ~6 mL/kg/min underestimate comes from mostly very fit samples. In Lambe 2025 all but one participant rated Good/Excellent/Superior. In Lambe 2026 the lower-fitness subgroup (≤70th percentile, n=10) had mean difference −2.41 (95% CI −5.28 to 0.47, not significant), vs −7.79 in the ≥80th-percentile group. Caserman 2024 (Apple Watch Series 7), cited by Lambe 2025, found overestimation in people with poor fitness. For a low-fitness user, do not apply a '~6 low' correction. Keep the symmetric ±7 band and read the trend.
corrections.source: Lambe 2026 full text (PMC13141568) subgroup analysis; Lambe 2025 Discussion (PMC12080799) citing Caserman et al. JMIR Biomed Eng 2024;9:e59459

corrections.claim: 28 studies, 723 adults, baseline 40.8±7.9; ET +4.9 (±1.4); HIIT +5.5 (±1.2); +3.2 at lower baseline; +3.0 longer interventions; HIIT vs ET +1.2 (±0.9)
corrections.correction: Confirmed. The ± values are 95% confidence limits, and the +3.2/+3.0 moderators apply to HIIT. For endurance training the lower-baseline moderator was only +1.4 (±2.0).

corrections.claim: 4×4 at 90–95% HRmax: +7.2% (55.5 → 60.4); 15/15 +5.5%; stroke volume ~+10%; 3×/wk, 8 wk, work-matched, moderately trained men
corrections.correction: Confirmed (n=40). 15/15 went 60.5 → 64.4. The protocol used a 10-min warm-up at ~70% HRmax and 3-min active rest at 70% HRmax.
corrections.source: Med Sci Sports Exerc 2007;39:665-71 (PDF linked in research)

corrections.correction: Confirmed (334 subjects, 40 training groups; longer intervals gave ~0.8–0.9 L/min).

corrections.claim: Intensity tertiles gave similar VO2max gains
corrections.correction: Confirmed: +0.29 / +0.26 / +0.35 L/min, no significant difference (28 studies).

corrections.claim: Non-response fell from 60 → 300 min/wk and disappeared with +120 min/wk
corrections.correction: Confirmed (n=78, 6-week blocks). Note that non-response was defined by maximal power output (Wmax), not VO2max.

corrections.claim: Evidence does not support Zone 2 as optimal; higher intensities critical especially at lower volumes
corrections.correction: Confirmed (narrative review).
Confirmed.

corrections.claim: 12 studies, 111,309 people; significant from 2,517 steps vs 2,000; optimum ~8,763 (aHR 0.40); CVD ~7,126; cadence independently protective; larger effects with hip vs wrist devices
corrections.correction: Confirmed: 2,517 (aHR 0.92); 8,763 (0.40); CVD 7,126 (0.49). The conclusion rounds these to ~2,600 and ~8,800.

corrections.claim: Wrist-worn devices undercount relative to the hip accelerometers used in some cohorts
corrections.correction: The direction is reversed. In free living, wrist-worn devices generally record MORE steps than hip-worn ones: research-grade wrist accelerometers ~15–30% more, consumer wrist devices ~3–15% more. They undercount only when the wrist is still, e.g. pushing a cart or stroller. Stens 2023 only reports stronger risk gradients with hip-worn accelerometers. If anything, placing wrist counts on hip-derived ladders may overstate where the user sits.
corrections.source: CDC Prev Chronic Dis 2022 (21_0343); Frontiers Med 2019 PMC6849483; Stens 2023 abstract

corrections.claim: 43 studies; SMD −0.06 max strength, −0.01 hypertrophy, −0.28 explosive; worse in the same session (p=0.043) than with ≥3 h separation
corrections.correction: Confirmed. Note that Schumann found NO significant moderator for cycling vs running; the running-specific interference comes from Wilson 2012 and Lundberg 2022. 'Rowing' is not examined in any cited source, so that part is unverifiable.

corrections.claim: 21 studies; hypertrophy ES 0.85 concurrent vs 1.23 strength-only; running not cycling caused decrements; frequency and duration negatively correlated
corrections.correction: Confirmed (422 effect sizes; correlations r −0.26 to −0.35 for frequency, −0.29 to −0.75 for duration).

corrections.claim: 15 studies; overall SMD −0.23 (−0.46 to −0.00); type I with running −0.81
corrections.correction: Confirmed: running type I −0.81 (−1.26 to −0.36). Overall type I was −0.34 (n.s.) and type II −0.13 (n.s.).

corrections.claim: 87 studies; RR per 10 bpm 1.17 (1.14–1.19) all-cause; also higher CHD, sudden cardiac death, heart failure, AF, stroke and cancer risk
corrections.correction: The all-cause figure is correct. AF is wrong in the list: the RR per 10 bpm was 0.97 (0.92–1.02), a J-shaped association, not a linear increase. Sudden cardiac death was borderline, 1.09 (1.00–1.18). CHD 1.07, HF 1.18, stroke 1.06, CVD 1.15, cancer 1.14.

corrections.claim: HRR ≤12 bpm at 1 min → RR of death 4.0 (3.0–5.2), independent of workload (≈4× risk)
corrections.correction: 4.0 (3.0–5.2) is the UNIVARIATE RR. After adjusting for age, sex, medications, perfusion defects, cardiac risk factors, resting HR, HR change during exercise and workload, the adjusted RR was 2.0 (95% CI 1.5–2.7). The 'independent of workload' finding belongs to the 2.0 figure, so the copy should say ~2× (adjusted). Population: 2,428 clinically referred adults, mean age 57.
corrections.source: N Engl J Med 1999;341:1351-7, PMID 10536127 (abstract + NEJM results text)

corrections.claim: 24-h, short-term and ultra-short HRV norms are not interchangeable
corrections.correction: Confirmed.

corrections.claim: Day-to-day HRV needs rolling averages and individual baselines; the same direction can mean different things
corrections.correction: Confirmed.

corrections.claim: Adults should regularly sleep ≥7 h
corrections.correction: Confirmed (AASM/SRS consensus).

corrections.claim: 69 publications, 227 outcomes; −7.56% (−11.9 to −3.13); significant for all categories; ~0.4%/h awake; PM affected, AM largely not
corrections.correction: Confirmed (89% male participants).

corrections.claim: n=10, 14-day deficit; 5.5 vs 8.5 h cut fat loss 55% (0.6 vs 1.4 kg) and raised FFM loss 60% (2.4 vs 1.5 kg)
corrections.correction: Confirmed. It was a randomized crossover in overweight, non-training adults (mean age 41, BMI 27.4), not lifters.

corrections.claim: n=13 crossover; one night without sleep: MPS −18%, cortisol +21%, testosterone −24%
corrections.correction: Confirmed (7 men, 6 women).

corrections.claim: 49 RCTs, 1,863 participants; no further FFM gain above 1.62 g/kg/day (CI ~1.03–2.20)
corrections.correction: The numbers are right: breakpoint 1.62 (95% CI 1.03–2.20) g/kg/day. But the biphasic model came from 42 study arms (723 participants) and was NOT statistically significant (p=0.079). The authors themselves suggest ~2.2 g/kg/day 'for those seeking to maximise' FFM gains. Present 1.6 as a floor, not a proven ceiling.
corrections.source: Br J Sports Med 2018, PMC5867436 full text (Figure 5 and Discussion)

corrections.claim: 0.4 g/kg per meal over ≥4 meals to reach ≥1.6 g/kg/day; up to 0.55 g/kg per meal at 2.2 g/kg/day
corrections.correction: Confirmed (narrative review).
corrections.source: J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2018, PMID 29497353

corrections.claim: 6 studies; energy-restricted lean trained athletes need 2.3–3.1 g/kg FFM
corrections.correction: Confirmed. 'Lean' was defined as ≤23% body fat for males.
corrections.source: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab 2014, PMID 24092765

corrections.claim: 4,637 healthy adults; age, waist, leisure activity and resting HR strongest predictors; 61% (men) and 56% (women) variance; SEE 5.70 and 5.14
corrections.correction: Confirmed. The final models included 2,067 men and 2,193 women.
